young.html: In the last parts of his great book, Thomas Aquinas wrote about seven virtues, seven strong good habits. Four of them help anyone live well: prudence (good sense), justice (fairness), fortitude (courage) and temperance (self-control). Three more he called the virtues that lead to God: faith, hope and charity, which means love.

young.name: gb-virtue-wheel
young.cap: Tap each virtue on the wheel. The inner ring holds faith, hope and charity; the outer ring holds the four "hinge" virtues.

young.html: Thomas said that charity is a kind of friendship with God. And just as you are kind to your best friend's little brother because you love your friend, charity is kind to everyone, even people who are hard to like.

Thomas worked on his book for years, writing and dictating to helpers. Near the end of his life he stopped writing, and the book was never finished. His friends finished the last pages using things he had written earlier.

A virtue week. Draw a circle and divide it into seven slices, one for each virtue. Each day, look for one example of a virtue, in a story you read, at home or at school, and write or draw it in its slice. Which slice filled up fastest? Which was hardest to spot?

full.html: Volume 18 of the set carries the Summa on from where the last rung stopped. The Second Part of the Second Part (in Latin, Secunda Secundae) takes the virtues one at a time: first the three theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, and then the four cardinal virtues, each with the vices opposed to it. The Third Part is about Christ and the sacraments. Aquinas stopped writing in December 1273, partway through the sacrament of penance; after his death his followers completed the work with a Supplement drawn from his earlier writings. This rung follows the selections in the set, which center on faith, hope and charity.

full.name: gb-virtue-wheel
full.cap: Seven virtues of the Second Part of the Second Part, with the questions that treat each and the vices set against them.

full.html: Aquinas defines faith with the Letter to the Hebrews: "the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things that appear not." Its object, he says, is God as the first truth. To believe is an act of the mind, which assents to what God has revealed, moved by the will. That is why faith differs from knowledge: what we see proved, we know; what we accept on another's word, we believe. He holds that the same thing cannot be both known and believed by the same person in the same respect.

full.text: It is therefore evident that hope is a virtue, since it causes a human act to be good and to attain its due rule.
full.work: Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 17, Article 1
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.html: Hope, for Aquinas, looks forward to a good that is future, hard to reach, but possible: eternal happiness with God, reached with God's help. It has two opposites. Despair gives up on that good; presumption takes it for granted. Like a moral virtue, hope steers between them.

Question 23 asks whether charity is friendship. Aquinas borrows Aristotle's account of friendship: a love that wishes the friend well, is returned, and rests on something the friends share. God, he holds, shares his own happiness with people.

full.text: The love which is based on this communication, is charity: wherefore it is evident that charity is the friendship of man for God.
full.work: Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 23, Article 1
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.title: Why charity is the greatest
full.q: Aquinas, with Paul's "the greatest of these is charity" (1 Corinthians 13:13), argues that charity is the highest virtue (Question 23, Article 6). Lay out his reasoning.
steps: The theological virtues are higher than the others, because they reach God himself.
Faith reaches God as a source of truth we do not yet see; hope reaches God as a good we do not yet have.
Charity reaches God as he is, resting in him, not in something still to come.
So charity is the greatest, and it directs all the other virtues to their last end, which is why he calls it their "form."
full.a: Charity, because it rests in God himself and gives every other virtue its direction.

full.html: The questions on charity are full of everyday matters. Charity loves God first, then oneself, then one's neighbor; it loves enemies too, in the sense of wishing them good and being ready to help. Its fruits are joy, peace, mercy, kindness and giving to those in need. Opposed to it are hatred, envy, discord and quarreling. In this same section Aquinas asks whether it is always wrong to wage war (Question 40), and gives the conditions that became the classic statement of "just war" teaching: the right authority, a just cause and a right intention. Writers on war and peace have debated these conditions ever since.

items: Prudence (Questions 47 to 56): practical wisdom, right reason about what to do.
Justice (Questions 57 to 122): giving each person what is due to them. Here Aquinas treats fair prices, honest lending, telling the truth, gratitude and religion as a part of justice.
Fortitude (Questions 123 to 140): firmness in danger, with patience and perseverance.
Temperance (Questions 141 to 170): keeping our desires within the measure that reason sets.

full.html: The Third Part asks why God became man and how, then turns to the sacraments, which Aquinas describes as signs that, as he believes, also bring about the grace they signify. He counts seven, matching them to the stages of a person's life, from birth (baptism) to illness and death. He presents all of this as the teaching of his faith, argued with the same objections and replies as the rest.

Picturing the Summa as a book of rules. It is a book of arguments. Even on faith and charity, Aquinas lists objections and answers them with reasons, and he often finds some truth in the view he rejects.

deep.html: On or near the feast of Saint Nicholas in December 1273, Aquinas stopped writing. His companion, Reginald of Piperno, later reported that when urged to go on, Thomas said that all he had written seemed like straw compared with what he had seen. The story comes from the testimony gathered for his canonization, and readers have taken it in many ways. He died on 7 March 1274 at the abbey of Fossanova, on his way to a church council in Lyon.

Aquinas also wrote poetry: he is traditionally credited with the Latin hymns for the feast of Corpus Christi, such as Pange lingua, still sung today. His account of the virtues shaped Dante's Divine Comedy, where Saints Peter, James and John examine Dante on faith, hope and charity, and it remains a reference point in moral philosophy, including the recent revival of "virtue ethics."

items: Aquinas says the same thing cannot be both known and believed by the same person. Do you agree? Can you believe something and also have good evidence for it?
Is hope a virtue, or only a feeling? Can it be practiced?
What does it mean to love an enemy? Is it the same as liking them?
Can a war ever be just? What would have to be true?

deep.html: Compare Aristotle on friendship in the Ethics, Augustine's City of God on the two loves, and later, Spinoza and Kant on what morality asks of us.

questions: Which of the seven virtues do you think is hardest? Which is easiest for you?
Aquinas says despair and presumption are both opposed to hope. Can you think of an example of each?
What makes a friendship? Use Aquinas's three marks: wishing each other well, love returned, something shared.
Why do you think Aquinas stopped writing before the book was done? What would you do with an unfinished project you loved?
Is it possible to be kind to someone you don't like? How?
care: This rung presents Thomas Aquinas's Christian teaching on faith, hope, charity and the sacraments as his own views, without arguing for or against them. It mentions his questions on war without detail.
